newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ saw scope for confusion under cash rate plan.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ saw scope for confusion under cash rate plan.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand officials said on Wednesday they had seen scope for misunderstanding of the bank's monetary policy signals under a conventional official cash rate system.

The bank announced two weeks ago it was ditching a plan to move to a cash rate policy targeting system, in the face of market opposition to ideas outlined in a discussion paper released by the RBNZ earlier in the year.
New Zealand's central bank is one of the few in the world not to have an official cash rate.

RBNZ Head of Financial Markets David Archer told a briefing that the bank's move in December to a more quantitative signalling system of desired monetary conditions meant there was potential confusion in setting a cash rate fortnightly.
The desired conditions are based on indicator 90-day bank bills and the New Zealand dollar Trade-Weighted Index (TWI).

Archer said it might have been hard for people unfamiliar with the system to understand that a call for easier interest rates did not necessarily signal a loosening of monetary conditions. The call might have been made simply to counterbalance a rise in the TWI.
"That probably was the single most important reason in our conclusion not to proceed with the cash rate system," he said.

Archer said the bank would continue to use both quantitative signals, giving the level of desired conditions, and qualititative signals, where the bank told markets conditions were tighter or looser than desired.
"The game is unchanged from the way we have been running it since December," Archer said.
The desired conditions would be used as a reference point.
Archer said the bank would continue to use RB bills and float tenders as previously "for the foreseeable future", but acknowledged there would be modications at some stage.
The bank would retain the daily cash target as its strongest signalling weapon.
"That remains the key thing we have at our disposal."
Archer accepted that markets would still attempt to second-guess the bank and players would attempt to work out what was an acceptable band of desired monetary conditions.
"There will be bandwidth issues," he said, adding that whatever system was used, traders would attempt to anticipate the central bank's next policy move.
